description: What does a pivot table do?
explanation: A pivot table summarises a large table by grouping rows on chosen fields and aggregating a value for each group.
choice0: Groups rows by chosen fields and aggregates a value for each group
choice1: Rotates the sheet so rows become columns
choice2: Removes duplicate rows from a table
choice3: Converts a table into a chart automatically

description: What must be true of your source data before a pivot table will work well?
explanation: Pivot tables expect a tidy rectangular table: one header row, one record per row, no blank or merged rows inside it.
choice0: It must be sorted alphabetically
choice1: It must contain only numbers
choice2: It needs one header row, one record per row and no blank or merged rows
choice3: It must be on the same sheet as the pivot table

description: In a pivot table, what does putting a field in the Rows area do?
explanation: Each distinct value of that field becomes its own row, and the values area is aggregated within it.
choice0: It filters the data to that field
choice1: It creates one row per distinct value of the field
choice2: It sorts the data by that field only
choice3: It hides the field from the summary

description: Why must a pivot table be refreshed after the source data changes?
explanation: A pivot table works from a cached snapshot of the source, so it does not update automatically.
choice0: Because pivot tables are always read-only
choice1: Because refreshing re-sorts the source data
choice2: Because the source range shrinks over time
choice3: Because it summarises a cached snapshot rather than the live data

description: What does changing a pivot value field from Sum to Count change?
explanation: The aggregation changes from adding the values to tallying how many records fall in each group.
choice0: It tallies how many records are in each group instead of totalling them
choice1: It sorts the groups by size
choice2: It removes empty groups
choice3: It converts the numbers to percentages

description: Why is INDEX and MATCH often preferred to VLOOKUP in a maintained model?
explanation: It does not depend on a fixed column offset, so inserting or moving a column does not silently break the formula.
choice0: It is the only method that handles text keys
choice1: It does not break when columns are inserted or moved
choice2: It can search several workbooks at once
choice3: It never returns an error

description: What does the fourth argument of MATCH being 0 mean?
explanation: A match type of 0 requires an exact match and works on unsorted data.
choice0: Return the first row of the range
choice1: Search backwards from the end
choice2: Require an exact match
choice3: Round the search value before matching

description: How can you perform a lookup on two conditions at once?
explanation: Combining the keys, or using a multi-condition function such as XLOOKUP with a concatenated key, matches on both fields.
choice0: Match on a combined key built from both fields
choice1: Run two separate VLOOKUPs and add the results
choice2: Sort the table by both fields first, which is enough on its own
choice3: It is not possible in a spreadsheet

description: What does an array formula do differently from an ordinary one?
explanation: It operates on whole ranges at once and can return several results, rather than working cell by cell.
choice0: It repeats the same value across a range
choice1: It works on entire ranges at once and can return multiple results
choice2: It runs only when the file is opened
choice3: It converts formulas into static values

description: What does a spill range mean in a modern spreadsheet?
explanation: One formula returns several values that automatically fill the neighbouring cells, and those cells cannot be occupied.
choice0: One formula fills several neighbouring cells with its results
choice1: A formula that overflows its column width
choice2: A formula copied to too many cells
choice3: A calculation that exceeds the row limit

description: What causes a #SPILL! error?
explanation: The formula needs to write into cells that already contain something, so it cannot lay out its results.
choice0: The formula is nested too deeply
choice1: The result is too large a number
choice2: Something already occupies the cells the result needs
choice3: Two formulas reference each other

description: Why can whole-column references such as A:A slow a large workbook?
explanation: They ask the engine to consider every row in the column, which multiplies the work when many formulas do it.
choice0: They use more disk space when saved
choice1: They make each formula consider every row in the column
choice2: They prevent the file from being sorted
choice3: They disable automatic recalculation

description: Why are volatile functions such as NOW and RAND worth limiting?
explanation: They recalculate on every change anywhere in the workbook, dragging every formula that depends on them along with them.
choice0: They recalculate on every change, forcing dependent formulas to recalculate too
choice1: They cannot be used inside IF statements
choice2: They return text rather than numbers
choice3: They are unavailable in shared workbooks

description: Why is it better to put an assumption such as a tax rate in its own cell than to type it into every formula?
explanation: One labelled input cell can be changed once and flows through the whole model, and it is visible for review.
choice0: It makes formulas calculate faster
choice1: Spreadsheets forbid literal numbers in formulas
choice2: It reduces the size of the file
choice3: The value can be changed in one place and is visible for review

description: What is the main risk of hardcoding a number inside a long formula?
explanation: It is invisible to anyone reading the sheet and easy to miss when the assumption changes, so results go quietly stale.
choice0: It hides an assumption that will later be missed when it changes
choice1: It always produces a #VALUE! error
choice2: It prevents the formula from being copied
choice3: It forces the workbook into manual calculation mode

description: What does a sensitivity or what-if table show you?
explanation: It recalculates an output across a grid of input values, showing how sensitive the result is to those assumptions.
choice0: Which cells changed most recently
choice1: How an output varies as one or two inputs change
choice2: Which formulas contain errors
choice3: How long the workbook takes to recalculate

description: What does =SUMPRODUCT(A1:A5, B1:B5) calculate?
explanation: It multiplies the two ranges element by element and adds the products, which is how a weighted total is built.
choice0: The sum of both ranges added together
choice1: The product of the two totals
choice2: The sum of each pair multiplied together
choice3: The largest product of any pair

description: Why is SUMPRODUCT a natural way to compute a weighted average numerator?
explanation: It pairs each value with its weight, multiplies, and totals the results in one step.
choice0: It multiplies each value by its weight and totals the results
choice1: It sorts the values by weight first
choice2: It ignores zero weights automatically
choice3: It divides by the number of items automatically

description: What does =IFS() offer over deeply nested IF functions?
explanation: IFS lists condition and result pairs in sequence, which is far easier to read and edit than nesting.
choice0: It evaluates all conditions simultaneously
choice1: It lists condition and result pairs in a flat, readable sequence
choice2: It allows conditions to reference other sheets
choice3: It removes the need for an else case

description: What does =UNIQUE() return from a column of values?
explanation: It returns each distinct value once, spilling the results into the cells below.
choice0: The most frequent value
choice1: The number of distinct values
choice2: The values sorted alphabetically
choice3: Each distinct value, once

description: What does =FILTER(A2:C50, B2:B50>100) return?
explanation: It returns the rows of the range where the condition is true, as a spilled result.
choice0: The rows where column B exceeds 100
choice1: The count of rows where column B exceeds 100
choice2: Column B with values over 100 highlighted
choice3: The range sorted by column B

description: What does =SORT() do that the sort command does not?
explanation: SORT is a formula, so its output updates automatically when the source data changes.
choice0: It sorts by more columns at once
choice1: Its result updates automatically as the source changes
choice2: It sorts without needing a header row
choice3: It sorts in place without a helper range

description: Why is a helper column often a good idea in a complex sheet?
explanation: Breaking a calculation into named intermediate steps makes it far easier to read, audit and correct.
choice0: It makes the workbook calculate faster in every case
choice1: It is required before creating a pivot table
choice2: It splits a complex calculation into readable, auditable steps
choice3: It prevents other users from editing the formula

description: What is the practical difference between a plain range and a formal table object?
explanation: A table names its columns, expands automatically as rows are added, and lets formulas refer to fields by name.
choice0: A table expands automatically and lets formulas use column names
choice1: A table cannot contain formulas
choice2: A range cannot be sorted
choice3: A table can only hold text

description: Why do structured references such as Sales[Amount] survive edits better than C2:C500?
explanation: They point at a named column, so inserting rows or moving columns does not leave the formula reading the wrong cells.
choice0: They calculate more quickly
choice1: They follow the named column rather than fixed cell positions
choice2: They are automatically absolute
choice3: They cannot produce errors

description: What is the weakness of relying on data validation alone to keep data clean?
explanation: Validation only checks values as they are typed, so pasted or imported data can bypass it entirely.
choice0: It slows the workbook down noticeably
choice1: It cannot restrict values to a list
choice2: It only works on numeric columns
choice3: Pasted or imported values can bypass it

description: What do the trace precedents and trace dependents tools show?
explanation: Precedents are the cells a formula reads; dependents are the cells that read it. Together they map the flow of a model.
choice0: Which cells a formula reads, and which cells read it
choice1: Which cells were changed most recently
choice2: Which formulas take longest to calculate
choice3: Which cells are protected

description: Why is it worth checking that a SUM range covers every intended row?
explanation: A total whose range stops short of the last rows is silently wrong, and nothing flags it as an error.
choice0: Because SUM cannot handle more than 1000 rows
choice1: Because SUM ignores negative numbers
choice2: Because a short range gives a wrong total with no error shown
choice3: Because SUM requires a sorted range

description: A total does not match the sum of its parts. What is a likely cause?
explanation: Numbers stored as text are skipped by SUM, so they are missing from the total while still being visible.
choice0: The cells are formatted with too few decimal places
choice1: Some values are stored as text and skipped by SUM
choice2: The sheet needs to be saved first
choice3: The column is too narrow

description: What is the difference between rounding a value with ROUND and just displaying fewer decimals?
explanation: ROUND changes the stored value, while decimal formatting changes only the display and leaves the full value in the calculation.
choice0: ROUND changes the stored value; formatting changes only the display
choice1: They are identical in effect
choice2: Formatting changes the value; ROUND changes only the display
choice3: ROUND works only on whole numbers

description: Why can a column of displayed values appear not to add up to its displayed total?
explanation: The total is computed from the full precision values, while each cell shows a rounded version, so the visible figures differ slightly.
choice0: Because the total uses a different function
choice1: Because hidden rows are excluded
choice2: Because the total is computed from unrounded values while each cell is displayed rounded
choice3: Because percentages cannot be totalled

description: Why do dates imported from a text file sometimes refuse to sort chronologically?
explanation: They arrived as text rather than date serial numbers, so they sort alphabetically instead.
choice0: The sort was applied to the wrong column
choice1: They are stored as text, so they sort alphabetically
choice2: Dates can only be sorted inside a pivot table
choice3: The date format is not supported

description: What does =EOMONTH(A1, 0) return?
explanation: EOMONTH returns the last day of the month, with the second argument shifting by that many months.
choice0: The last day of the month containing the date in A1
choice1: The first day of the month containing the date in A1
choice2: The number of days in the month
choice3: Todays date

description: What does =NETWORKDAYS(start, end) return?
explanation: It counts the working days between two dates, excluding weekends and any holidays supplied.
choice0: The total number of days between the dates
choice1: The number of weekends between the dates
choice2: The number of weeks between the dates
choice3: The number of working days between the dates

description: How would you extract the part of an email address before the at sign?
explanation: FIND locates the at sign and LEFT takes everything up to one character before it.
choice0: Use MID with a fixed starting position
choice1: Use TRIM and then UPPER
choice2: Use FIND to locate the at sign, then LEFT to take the characters before it
choice3: Use RIGHT with the length of the domain

description: What does the wildcard character * mean in a COUNTIF criterion?
explanation: An asterisk stands for any run of characters, so "north*" matches anything starting with north.
choice0: Any sequence of characters
choice1: Exactly one character
choice2: A literal asterisk
choice3: A numeric digit

description: What does the wildcard character ? mean in a criterion?
explanation: A question mark matches exactly one character in that position.
choice0: Any sequence of characters
choice1: Exactly one character
choice2: The end of the text
choice3: An optional character

description: What does protecting a sheet while leaving some cells unlocked achieve?
explanation: Users can edit only the input cells you left unlocked, while formulas and structure stay safe.
choice0: Users can edit only the cells you left unlocked
choice1: The file cannot be opened without a password
choice2: The sheet becomes entirely read-only
choice3: Formulas are converted to values

description: What is the main risk of several people editing one shared workbook at once?
explanation: Simultaneous edits can conflict, and one persons change can overwrite anothers without either noticing.
choice0: The file grows too large to open
choice1: Formulas stop recalculating
choice2: Conflicting edits can silently overwrite one another
choice3: Charts are removed automatically

description: When is a scatter plot the right choice?
explanation: A scatter plot shows the relationship between two numeric variables, one on each axis.
choice0: When comparing a total across categories
choice1: When showing how two numeric variables relate
choice2: When showing parts of a whole
choice3: When tracking one value over evenly spaced time

description: What does adding a secondary axis to a chart let you do, and what is the risk?
explanation: It lets two series on different scales share a chart, but the independent scales can imply a relationship that is not there.
choice0: Plot two different scales together, at the risk of implying a false relationship
choice1: Show more categories than one axis allows
choice2: Convert a bar chart into a line chart
choice3: Display a chart on two sheets at once

description: Why should you check for blank cells before averaging a column?
explanation: AVERAGE ignores blanks, so a column with gaps averages over fewer values than you may expect.
choice0: Blanks are treated as zero and drag the average down
choice1: AVERAGE refuses to run when blanks are present
choice2: Blanks are treated as one and inflate the average
choice3: AVERAGE skips blanks, so the divisor is smaller than the row count

description: How do zeros and blanks differ when averaging?
explanation: A zero is a value and is included in the mean, while a blank is skipped entirely, so the two give different answers.
choice0: A zero is included in the mean, a blank is skipped
choice1: Both are skipped
choice2: Both are included
choice3: A zero is skipped, a blank is included

description: What does a running total column show?
explanation: Each row shows the cumulative sum of everything up to and including that row.
choice0: The average of the values so far
choice1: The cumulative sum up to and including that row
choice2: The difference from the previous row
choice3: The percentage of the grand total

description: How do you express a value as a percentage of a column total in a way that survives being copied down?
explanation: Divide the row value by an absolute reference to the total cell, so the denominator never shifts.
choice0: Divide by the cell directly above
choice1: Divide by a relative reference to the total
choice2: Divide by an absolute reference to the total cell
choice3: Multiply by 100 and format as text

description: Why is wrapping every formula in IFERROR a questionable habit?
explanation: It hides genuine mistakes as well as expected ones, so a broken formula looks like a legitimate blank.
choice0: It hides real errors as well as expected ones
choice1: It slows recalculation considerably
choice2: It only works on lookup functions
choice3: It converts numbers into text

description: A lookup returns #N/A for a few rows only. What is the most likely cause?
explanation: Those particular keys have no match, often because of stray spaces, differing case handling or a text-versus-number mismatch.
choice0: The lookup range is locked
choice1: Those keys have no match, often due to stray spaces or a text-number mismatch
choice2: The formula was not copied far enough
choice3: The workbook needs to be saved

description: Why is it good practice to separate raw data, calculations and presentation onto different sheets?
explanation: Keeping the layers apart means the raw data can be refreshed without disturbing the formulas or the report layout.
choice0: It makes the file open faster
choice1: It is required for pivot tables to work
choice2: Raw data can be refreshed without disturbing formulas or the report layout
choice3: It prevents formulas from referencing other sheets

description: What does documenting a workbook with a notes or assumptions sheet achieve?
explanation: It records where the data came from and what the model assumes, so someone else, or you later, can trust and check the numbers.
choice0: It records sources and assumptions so the numbers can be checked later
choice1: It reduces the file size
choice2: It locks the assumptions against change
choice3: It is required before sharing a workbook

description: What is a reasonable first step when you inherit a spreadsheet you did not build?
explanation: Trace the outputs back to their inputs to learn what the model actually does before changing anything.
choice0: Delete unused sheets immediately
choice1: Trace the key outputs back to their inputs to understand the model
choice2: Convert every formula to a value
choice3: Re-sort every table alphabetically
